node-1.label: Patient developed fever, erythematous maculopapular eruption with keratosis pilaris on limbs and trunk, and facial photosensitivity on day 9 of treatment

node-2.label: Patient is a man in his 70s with stage IV melanoma with hepatic and lymph node metastasis, receiving vemurafenib 960 mg twice daily as first-line treatment

node-3.label: Fever with body temperature 38.6°C (101.5°F) occurred on day 9 of treatment

node-4.label: Physical examination showed erythematous maculopapular eruption with keratosis pilaris on all 4 limbs and trunk involving 30% of body surface area, and photosensitivity on the face

why.why: New laboratory findings of 12% eosinophilia and 2% atypical lymphocytes support a drug hypersensitivity reaction and are consistent with a vemurafenib-induced cutaneous reaction. Normal liver enzymes reduce concern for DRESS but do not refute the diagnosis, and electrolyte wasting is non-refuting. Both the Laboratory Physician and Pathologist analyses explicitly support vemurafenib cutaneous reaction as the most probable diagnosis, so confidence increased from 0.8 to 0.92.

The new lab results showing eosinophilia and atypical lymphocytes favor a drug hypersensitivity reaction rather than infection. The absence of infectious exposure or positive cultures, emphasized by expert analyses, makes infection unlikely, and the photosensitivity and keratosis pilaris are atypical for an infectious rash. Confidence decreased from 0.15 to 0.05.

New findings of eosinophilia and atypical lymphocytes point toward drug-related hypersensitivity, and expert analyses reaffirm that the clinical features and day-9 timing align with vemurafenib rather than a paraneoplastic process. The skin findings are not typical paraneoplastic manifestations, so confidence decreased from 0.05 to 0.02.

node-11.label: Laboratory tests show renal electrolyte wasting

node-12.label: No infectious exposure or positive cultures have been identified

node-13.label: Patient has drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) syndrome

attrs.why: Fever, maculopapular rash, eosinophilia, atypical lymphocytes, and renal electrolyte wasting overlap with DRESS features, but normal liver enzymes reduce concern for DRESS, and expert analyses specifically note that severe DRESS is not supported. Therefore confidence is low at 0.12.
